glossary.definition: A ray is an infinitely thin line showing the path along which light energy travels when wavelength goes to zero.
glossary.example: A narrow laser beam in air travels along a straight ray.

glossary.definition: Geometrical optics is the study of light propagation using rays by neglecting the tiny finite wavelength of light.
glossary.example: Tracing rays through eyeglasses or a camera lens uses geometrical optics.

glossary.definition: Diffraction is the spreading of light at the edges of a very small opening because light has a finite wavelength.
glossary.example: A hole smaller than 0.1 mm blurs the sharp shadow on a screen.

glossary.definition: The refractive index n of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum c to its speed v in that medium.
glossary.example: Glass with n = 1.5 slows light to c / 1.5.

glossary.definition: A homogeneous medium is a material whose refractive index has the same constant value at every point.
glossary.example: Calm air at uniform temperature is a homogeneous medium.

glossary.definition: Optical path length is the geometric distance light travels multiplied by the refractive index of the medium.
glossary.example: Travelling 2 cm in glass of n = 1.5 gives an optical path length of 3 cm.

glossary.definition: A stationary path is a path whose travel time does not change to first order when the path is slightly shifted.
glossary.example: At the bottom of a smooth valley, a tiny step sideways does not change height.

glossary.definition: Fermat's principle states that a light ray between two points follows a path whose optical path length is stationary.
glossary.example: Light bends at water so the total travel time stays stationary.

glossary.definition: Refraction is the bending of a light ray when it crosses the boundary between two media of different refractive indices.
glossary.example: A spoon in a glass of water looks bent at the water surface.

glossary.definition: The paraxial approximation restricts rays to small angles with the optical axis so sin θ and tan θ equal θ in radians.
glossary.example: For an angle of 0.05 rad, sin 0.05 is very close to 0.05.

glossary.definition: The center of curvature C is the center of the sphere of which a curved mirror or lens surface forms a part.
glossary.example: A normal line drawn at any point on a spherical surface passes through C.

glossary.definition: A meridional ray is a ray that stays inside a single flat plane containing the optical axis.
glossary.example: Any ray starting from a point on the optical axis is a meridional ray.

glossary.definition: A thin lens is a lens whose thickness is very small compared to the object distance, image distance, and surface radii.
glossary.example: A thin spectacle lens allows all distances to be measured from its center P.

glossary.definition: A principal focus is an axial point paired with rays parallel to the axis either after or before passing through the lens.
glossary.example: Sunlight parallel to the axis meets at the second principal focus F₂.

glossary.definition: Lateral magnification m is the ratio of the transverse image height y' to the transverse object height y.
glossary.example: If a 1 cm object forms an inverted 2 cm image, the lateral magnification is -2.

cards.label: 01 · §3.1 Definition
cards.title: What is geometrical optics?
cards.body: Geometrical optics treats light propagation using thin rays by neglecting the finite wavelength of light when apertures are large.

cards.title: Why denser media count as longer paths
cards.meaning: Optical path length is the vacuum distance that light would travel in the same time it takes to cross a medium.

cards.example: In glass with refractive index n = 1.5, a physical thickness of 2 cm has an optical path length of 1.5 × 2 cm = 3 cm.
cards.bridge: Because speed in a medium is c / n, the time for step ds is (n ds) / c, so integrating n ds gives the optical path length.

cards.label: 02 · §3.1 Definition
cards.title: What is optical path length?
cards.body: Optical path length is the integral of refractive index n along the geometric path, equal to c times the travel time.

cards.title: How light chooses its path
cards.meaning: Fermat's principle says light travels along a path whose travel time is stationary compared with slightly different nearby paths.

cards.label: 03 · §3.1 Definition
cards.title: What is Fermat's principle?
cards.body: Fermat's principle states that the actual ray path between two points makes the optical path length stationary with respect to small path variations.

steps.note: Write total optical path length from \(A\) to \(B\) via point \(R\) on \(PQ\).
In right triangle \(AMR\), replace \(AR\) with \(\sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\).
In right triangle \(RBN\), replace \(RB\) with \(\sqrt{(L - x)^2 + h_2^2}\) (Eq. 3.4).
Differentiate \(L_{op}\) with respect to \(x\); the chain rule on \((L - x)^2\) gives a minus sign.

ask.q: How do we find the stationary ray path as \(x\) varies?
ask.why: Fermat's principle requires differentiating the optical path with respect to \(x\).

steps.note: Set \(dL_{op}/dx = 0\) for an extremum optical path (Eq. 3.5).

ask.q: What value must \(dL_{op}/dx\) take on the actual ray path?
ask.why: At a stationary point of the optical path, the first derivative vanishes.

steps.note: In right triangle \(AMR\), substitute \(\sin\theta_1 = x/\sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\).

ask.q: What does \(x / \sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\) equal in triangle \(AMR\)?
ask.why: Side \(MR = x\) is opposite \(\theta_1\) and \(AR = \sqrt{x^2 + h_1^2}\) is the hypotenuse.

steps.note: In right triangle \(RBN\), substitute \(\sin\theta_2 = (L - x)/\sqrt{(L - x)^2 + h_2^2}\).
Add \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) to both sides.

ask.q: Which move places the two refraction terms on opposite sides?
ask.why: Adding \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) isolates \(n_2\sin\theta_2\) on the left and \(n_1\sin\theta_1\) on the right.

steps.note: Swap sides to obtain Snell's law of refraction (Eq. 3.6).

cards.label: 06 · §3.2 Examples
cards.title: Paraboloidal and elliptical reflectors (Examples 3.1–3.2)
cards.body: A paraboloid reflects parallel rays to its focus \(S\) (radio telescopes). An elliptical reflector sends every ray from focus \(S_1\) to focus \(S_2\) with stationary (constant) travel time (ruby laser).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: When does geometrical optics accurately describe light propagation?
options: When wavelength is much smaller than apertures
When apertures are smaller than wavelength
Only when refractive index is zero
cards.why: Neglecting wavelength works when openings are much larger than the wavelength of light.

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: According to the modern Fermat's principle, the optical path of a ray is:
cards.why: The ray path makes the optical path length stationary: a minimum, maximum, or constant.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: In a homogeneous medium, light rays travel along ______ lines.
cards.why: With constant refractive index, a straight line minimizes the optical path between two points.

cards.label: Quiz · Number
cards.q: Find the optical path length for \(4\text{ cm}\) in glass of \(n = 1.5\).
cards.why: Optical path length equals \(n \times d = 1.5 \times 4\text{ cm} = 6\text{ cm}\).

phases.name: Snell's law
phases.why: start from Snell's law and apply the paraxial approximation

phases.name: Incident angle
phases.why: express φ₁ from exterior angle of triangle OSC

phases.name: Refracted angle
phases.why: express φ₂ from exterior angle of triangle ISC

phases.name: Cancel height
phases.why: divide by h and collect distance terms

phases.name: Sign convention
phases.why: apply u = -x, v = y, and R = r

steps.note: Start from Snell's law at point \(S\) on spherical surface \(SPM\) (Eq. 4.1).
Use the paraxial approximation \(\sin\phi \approx \phi\) for small angles in radians.

ask.q: Why can \(\sin\phi_1\) and \(\sin\phi_2\) be replaced by \(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\)?
options: The surface is a plane mirror
ask.why: In the paraxial approximation, all angles in radians are small so \(\sin\phi \approx \phi\).

steps.note: In triangle \(OSC\), exterior angle \(\phi_1\) equals \(\beta + \alpha_1\).

ask.q: In triangle \(OSC\), what does exterior angle \(\phi_1\) equal?
ask.why: Angle \(\phi_1\) is exterior to interior angles \(\alpha_1\) at \(O\) and \(\beta\) at \(C\).

steps.note: Substitute \(\beta \approx \tan\beta = h/r\) and \(\alpha_1 \approx \tan\alpha_1 = h/x\) (Eq. 4.2).
In triangle \(ISC\), exterior angle \(\beta = \phi_2 + \alpha_2\), so \(\phi_2 = \beta - \alpha_2\).
Substitute \(\beta \approx h/r\) and \(\alpha_2 \approx \tan\alpha_2 = h/y\) (Eq. 4.3).
Divide both sides by \(h\) so the ray height cancels out.

ask.q: Why does dividing by \(h\) show all paraxial rays focus together?
options: The equation no longer depends on \(h\)
ask.why: Once \(h\) cancels, every paraxial ray gives the same image distance \(y\).

steps.note: Collect \(x, y\) terms on the left and \(r\) terms on the right (Eq. 4.4).
Apply the sign convention \(u = -x, v = y, R = r\) to get the Gaussian formula (Eq. 4.5).

ask.q: Since object \(O\) lies left of pole \(P\), what replaces \(x\)?
ask.why: Distances to the left of \(P\) are negative, so \(u = -x\) and \(x = -u\).

phases.name: Reflection law
phases.why: equate angles of incidence and reflection at S

phases.name: Incident ray
phases.why: write φ₁ from triangle OSC and paraxial ratios

phases.name: Reflected ray
phases.why: write φ₂ from triangle CSI and paraxial ratios

phases.name: Cancel height
phases.why: divide by h and collect 1/x + 1/y

phases.name: Sign convention
phases.why: substitute u = -x, v = -y, R = -r

steps.note: At point \(S\), the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
In triangle \(OSC\), exterior angle \(\beta = \alpha_1 + \phi_1\), so \(\phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1\).

ask.q: In triangle \(OSC\), how is \(\phi_1\) related to \(\beta\) and \(\alpha_1\)?
ask.why: Exterior angle \(\beta\) equals \(\alpha_1 + \phi_1\), so \(\phi_1 = \beta - \alpha_1\).

steps.note: Replace small angles \(\beta\) and \(\alpha_1\) by \(h/r\) and \(h/x\).
In triangle \(CSI\), exterior angle \(\alpha_2 = \beta + \phi_2\), so \(\phi_2 = \alpha_2 - \beta\).
Replace small angles \(\alpha_2\) and \(\beta\) by \(h/y\) and \(h/r\).

ask.q: What replaces \(\alpha_2\) in the paraxial approximation?
ask.why: Reflected ray \(SI\) meets the axis at distance \(y\), so \(\alpha_2 \approx h / y\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by \(h\).

ask.q: What is the next step to eliminate the ray height \(h\)?
ask.why: Every term has \(h\) in the numerator, so dividing by \(h\) removes it.

steps.note: Collect \(1/x + 1/y\) on the left and \(2/r\) on the right (Eq. 4.6).
Since \(O, I, C\) lie to the left of \(P\), substitute \(x = -u, y = -v, r = -R\).
Negate both sides to obtain the mirror equation (Eq. 4.7).

ask.q: Which substitution in the refraction formula also gives the mirror equation?
ask.why: Setting \(n_2 = -n_1\) in Eq. (4.5) turns Snell's law into reflection and yields Eq. (4.7).

cards.title: What is a thin spherical lens?
cards.body: A thin spherical lens is a medium bounded by two spherical refracting surfaces whose thickness t is very small compared to object, image, and curvature distances.

phases.name: First surface
phases.why: refraction at R₁ from n₁ into n₂ forms image Q at v'

phases.name: Second surface
phases.why: refraction at R₂ from n₂ into n₁ takes Q at v' to I at v

phases.name: Combine surfaces
phases.why: add the two surface equations to eliminate v'

phases.name: Relative index
phases.why: divide by n₁ and define n = n₂ / n₁

phases.name: Focal length
phases.why: define focal length f by Lensmaker's formula

steps.note: First surface \(R_1\) refracts light from \(n_1\) into \(n_2\), forming \(Q\) at \(v'\) (Eq. 4.8).
Point \(Q\) at \(v'\) acts as object for second surface \(R_2\) from \(n_2\) into \(n_1\) (Eq. 4.9).

ask.q: For the second surface \(R_2\), what acts as its object distance?
ask.why: The image \(Q\) formed by the first surface at \(v'\) serves as the object for the second surface.

steps.note: Add Eqs. (4.8) and (4.9) so \(+n_2/v'\) and \(-n_2/v'\) cancel out.

ask.q: Why do we add Eqs. (4.8) and (4.9) together?
ask.why: Adding \(+n_2/v'\) and \(-n_2/v'\) eliminates the intermediate image position \(v'\).

steps.note: Factor \((n_2 - n_1)\) on the right, flipping the sign on \(1/R_2\).

ask.q: When \((n_2 - n_1)\) is factored out of \((n_1 - n_2)/R_2\), what remains?
ask.why: Since \(n_1 - n_2 = -(n_2 - n_1)\), factoring out \((n_2 - n_1)\) leaves \(-1/R_2\).

steps.note: Divide both sides by surrounding refractive index \(n_1\).
Write \(n = n_2 / n_1\) to obtain the thin lens formula (Eq. 4.10).
Define focal length \(f\) by Eq. (4.12) to get Eq. (4.11).

ask.q: When \(u = -\infty\) (incident parallel rays), what does \(v\) equal?
ask.why: Setting \(1/u = 0\) in \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) gives \(v = f\).

cards.label: 04 · §4.5 Definition
cards.title: What are the first and second principal foci?
cards.body: The first principal focus F₁ is the axial object point whose refracted rays emerge parallel (v = ∞), and the second principal focus F₂ is the axial image point for incident parallel rays (u = -∞).

cards.label: 05 · §4.5 Ray tracing

cards.label: 06 · §4.5 Different media
cards.title: Thin lens with different media on its two sides (Eqs. 4.14–4.16)
cards.body: When medium \(n_1\) is on the left and \(n_3\) on the right, setting \(v = \infty\) (Eq. 4.15) and \(u = -\infty\) (Eq. 4.16) gives \(f_2 / f_1 = -n_3 / n_1\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: For a converging lens in air, what are the signs of \(f_1\) and \(f_2\)?
cards.why: For a converging lens, \(F_1\) lies on the left (\(f_1 < 0\)) and \(F_2\) lies on the right (\(f_2 > 0\)).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: How does a glass biconvex lens behave inside a liquid of higher refractive index?
cards.why: When \(n_2 < n_1\), \((n - 1)\) becomes negative, so \(f < 0\) and the biconvex lens diverges light.

cards.label: Quiz · Fill in
cards.q: A paraxial ray passing through the center \(P\) of a thin lens travels ______.
cards.why: At \(u = 0\), the thin lens formula gives \(v = 0\), so the ray through \(P\) passes undeviated.

phases.why: use similar triangles AOF₁ and LPF₁ at F₁

phases.name: Second focus
phases.why: use similar triangles KPF₂ and BIF₂ at F₂

phases.why: equate the two height ratios and cross-multiply

phases.name: Same medium
phases.why: set f₁ = -f and f₂ = f for the same surrounding medium

steps.note: Similar right triangles \(AOF_1\) and \(LPF_1\) share the angle at \(F_1\) (Eq. 4.17).
Cancel the minus signs in the numerator and denominator on the right.

move.label: Use similar triangles KPF₂ and BIF₂ (Eq. 4.18)

steps.note: In similar triangles \(KPF_2\) and \(BIF_2\) around \(F_2\), \(-y'/y = x_2/f_2\) (Eq. 4.18).

ask.q: In triangles \(KPF_2\) and \(BIF_2\), what does \(-y' / y\) equal?
ask.why: Since \(KP = y\) and \(BI = -y'\), the ratio of heights equals \(x_2 / f_2\).

steps.note: Equate the two expressions for \(-y'/y\) from Eqs. (4.17) and (4.18).
Multiply both sides by \(x_1 f_2\) to get the Newtonian lens formula (Eq. 4.19).

ask.q: Which move clears both denominators in \(f_1/x_1 = x_2/f_2\)?
ask.why: Multiplying by \(x_1 f_2\) gives \(f_1 f_2 = x_1 x_2\).

steps.note: When both sides have the same medium, Eq. (4.13) gives \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = f\).

ask.q: When the same medium surrounds the lens, what is \(f_1 f_2\)?
ask.why: Because \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = +f\), their product is \(-f^2\).

steps.note: Thus \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) must always have opposite signs (Eq. 4.20).

ask.q: Since \(x_1 x_2 = -f^2 < 0\), what must be true of \(x_1\) and \(x_2\)?
ask.why: A negative product \(-f^2\) means one lies left of its focus and the other lies right.

cards.example: A positive magnification (m > 0) means an erect image; a negative magnification (m < 0) means an inverted image.
cards.bridge: For a thin lens in one medium, similar triangles through pole P give m = y' / y = v / u = -f₁ / x₁ = -x₂ / f₂.

cards.label: 03 · §4.7 Definition
cards.title: What is lateral magnification?
cards.body: Lateral magnification m is the ratio of image height y' to object height y, where positive m means erect and negative m means inverted (Eq. 4.21).

phases.name: Triangles at C
phases.why: use similar triangles AOC and ICB through center C

phases.name: Surface law
phases.why: substitute v/R and u/R from the Gaussian surface equation

phases.name: First lens surface
phases.why: write magnification m₁ for the first surface of a thin lens

phases.name: Second lens surface
phases.why: write magnification m₂ for the second surface of a thin lens

phases.name: Total magnification
phases.why: multiply m₁ and m₂ to get m = v/u

steps.note: Ray \(ACB\) along the normal at \(C\) passes undeviated, giving similar triangles \(AOC\) and \(ICB\) (Eq. 4.22).

move.label: Divide numerator and denominator by R

steps.note: Divide numerator and denominator on the right-hand side by \(R\) (Eq. 4.22).

ask.q: Why does the ray from \(A\) through \(C\) pass straight without bending?
options: It hits the spherical surface along the normal
ask.why: Any line through center of curvature \(C\) is normal to the sphere, so \(\phi_1 = \phi_2 = 0\).

steps.note: Substitute \(v/R - 1\) and \(-u/R + 1\) from Eq. (4.5).
Negate both sides and set \(m = y'/y\) for a single refracting surface (Eq. 4.23).

ask.q: What is the lateral magnification of a single surface from \(n_1\) to \(n_2\)?
ask.why: Refraction from \(n_1\) into \(n_2\) gives \(m = (n_1 v)/(n_2 u)\) (Eq. 4.23).

steps.note: For the first surface of a thin lens (\(n_1 \to n_2\)), intermediate image at \(v'\) has magnification \(m_1\).
For the second surface (\(n_2 \to n_1\)), object at \(v'\) forms image at \(v\) with magnification \(m_2\).

ask.q: How is total magnification \(m\) found for two surfaces in succession?
ask.why: The first image height is scaled again by \(m_2\), so total magnification is \(m_1 m_2\).

steps.tex: m_1 m_2 = \frac{n_1 v'}{n_2 u}\cdot\frac{n_2 v}{n_1 v'}
steps.note: Multiply the two surface magnifications \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) together.
Cancel \(n_1, n_2\) and \(v'\) to get \(m = m_1 m_2 = v/u\) (Eq. 4.24).

ask.q: Which factors cancel when \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are multiplied?
ask.why: Factors \(n_1, n_2\) and intermediate image distance \(v'\) cancel, leaving \(m = v/u\).

cards.label: 05 · §4.7 Example
cards.title: Two thin lenses separated by 8 cm (Example 4.3)
cards.body: Convex lens (\(f = +20\text{ cm}\)) with \(u = -40\text{ cm}\) gives \(v_1 = +40\text{ cm}, m_1 = -1\). Concave lens (\(f = -10\text{ cm}\)) 8 cm behind has virtual object \(u_2 = +32\text{ cm}\), giving \(v \approx -14.5\text{ cm}\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What is Newton's lens formula when the same medium is on both sides?
cards.why: With the same medium on both sides, \(f_1 = -f\) and \(f_2 = f\), so \(x_1 x_2 = f_1 f_2 = -f^2\).

cards.label: Quiz · OMR
cards.q: What does a negative lateral magnification \(m < 0\) indicate?
cards.why: Since \(m = y'/y\), a negative value means \(y'\) and \(y\) have opposite signs (inverted).
